summary:
New Brunswick sets its own schools policy on sexual orientation and gender identity inside the Canadian legal framework. Policy 713, issued by the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development, has been in force since 17 August 2020 and was revised on 1 July 2023, 23 August 2023 and 1 January 2025.

In the version effective 1 January 2025, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them in informal school settings; parental consent is encouraged but not required. Formal records for students under 16 still require parental consent. The revision went further than the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

The policy's application clause covers the school environment and names all students together with school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors, so its rules reach adults present in New Brunswick classrooms who do not live in the province.

From 1 July 2023 until the January 2025 revision, the policy barred teachers from using the chosen name and pronouns of a student under 16 without parental consent, reversing a three-year-old rule that required teachers to obtain the student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. The 1 July 2023 change also dropped explicit wording letting students take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. Premier Blaine Higgs's Progressive Conservative government made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two were removed, and eight party members including six cabinet ministers sat out question period in June 2023 to protest the lack of process. Dissidents called for a leadership review. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick "need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians".

The proposed changes drew public opposition before they took effect: about 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the review, and Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review was under way. Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, told the rally that "we know it saves lives" and warned that "with this policy changed or removed, we're going to lose kids".

The policy as adopted in 2020 requires schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 parental-consent rule.
tangentialFactors:
New Brunswick's parental-consent dispute was settled by executive policy rather than by statute: the Higgs government amended Policy 713 without a legislative vote, and no notwithstanding clause was invoked. Two other provinces took the legislative route. Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023, invoking the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask schools to use their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and that act drew legal action by human rights groups. Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which were challenged in Alberta courts and then shielded from those challenges by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, also using the notwithstanding clause.

The New Brunswick dispute produced sustained intra-party and intergovernmental turbulence: two cabinet ministers quit over the 2023 changes, two were pushed out, party dissidents demanded a leadership review, and the Prime Minister publicly intervened on the safety of trans children in the province. The Holt government's 1 January 2025 revision reversed the 2023 consent rule and drew coverage framing it as going beyond the child advocate's recommendations.
localsOnly:
For New Brunswick families, the operative split in Policy 713 is between informal and formal records. A student of any age may set the name and pronouns used informally at school without parental consent under the version effective 1 January 2025, while any change to formal records for a student under 16 requires parental consent.

The policy binds school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents and volunteers as well as students, so the naming, pronoun and bathroom provisions govern the conduct of adults working in or visiting New Brunswick schools, not only teachers.

The 2023 parental-consent rule is the subject of a constitutional challenge brought by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association; the record does not state how that challenge was decided.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association's constitutional challenge to the 2023 parental-consent rule is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Whether the 1 July 2023 removal of explicit wording on taking part in extracurricular activities and sports teams reflecting a student's gender identity was restored by the 1 January 2025 revision is not documented in this inventory.

No New Brunswick provincial-jail placement rule for transgender detainees is documented here; rules for people held in federal custody are carried by the national record. Provincial correctional policies vary across Canada and New Brunswick's own is not sourced.

No New Brunswick-specific rules on changing a gender marker on provincial documents, and no New Brunswick human rights complaint procedure, appear in this inventory; the general provincial human rights framework is carried at the national level.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence, homicide or survey data for New Brunswick, and no dated incident record for the province.
